title: InP DFB lasers — patents, products, and the case for chokepoint pricing
body:
The IP density question is the right place to start, because the entire investment case for Sivers rests on it. If Sivers holds a genuine chokepoint in the laser supply chain for co-packaged optics, it commands pricing power and customer stickiness. If it doesn't — if sufficiently motivated competitors can replicate its InP DFB process within a product cycle — then it's simply a modestly sized fabricator with a temporarily favorable order book.

The patent portfolio offers one data point, albeit an incomplete one. Public patent databases show Sivers Photonics holding three issued patents and 16 applications pending across US, UK, Canada, and WIPO jurisdictions. The USPTO has issued patents including *Distributed feedback laser having enhanced etch stop features* and *Method of making an InP-based DFB laser* — both titles signalling process-level IP rather than end-product claims. The company describes itself as "one of the world's most advanced designer[s] (and small scale manufacturer) of customised III-V lasers," a characterization drawn from its own corporate literature.

Against this, consider the competitive baseline: Coherent and Lumentum each hold hundreds of issued laser patents. Measured by count alone, Sivers' 19 total filings look thin. But that comparison misfires. Coherent and Lumentum built their portfolios around volume production of standard telecom lasers — DWDM line cards, transceiver modules. That IP doesn't meaningfully cover what Sivers is doing: continuous-wave InP DFB designs optimized for the high-power, narrow-linewidth requirements of silicon photonics integration, specifically in the C-band (1530–1565nm) window required for co-packaged optics in AI datacenter switches.

## The Three-Layer Technical Stack

To understand why the IP picture matters differently here, you need to understand what Sivers actually builds. The chokepoint isn't a single component — it's the integrated capability to execute across three distinct technical disciplines simultaneously.

First, III-V epitaxial growth: indium phosphide is a compound semiconductor grown in MBE or MOCVD systems where temperature, pressure, and precursor chemistry tolerances are measured in fractions of a percent. The defect density of the epitaxial layer determines laser lifetime. Most university labs can grow InP; very few do so at device-grade quality for high-power telecom applications. Second, DFB grating fabrication: the distributed feedback grating is the optical feedback structure that makes a DFB laser single-mode — essential for coherent integration with silicon photonics. Etching gratings at nanometer-scale periodicity into InP requires electron-beam lithography and a process consistent enough to produce predictable wavelengths across a wafer. The *enhanced etch stop features* in Sivers' issued patent title points squarely at this fabrication step. Third, InP-on-silicon-photonics integration: attaching or butt-coupling an InP die to a silicon photonics waveguide introduces mode mismatch, thermal expansion coefficient differences, and alignment tolerances that determine insertion loss.

Sivers' collaboration with [imec](https://www.imec-int.com/), begun in 2019, addresses this third layer directly. Imec is the European reference centre for silicon photonics process development; its decision to use Sivers Photonics as the laser-supply partner for its C-band InP integration platform is a structural third-party endorsement. Imec sets the technical standards the rest of the European silicon photonics ecosystem follows.

## Where the Patents Don't Tell the Whole Story

The candid answer to the IP defensibility question is that three issued patents is a narrow disclosed moat, and Sivers itself likely knows it.

What matters more, in specialty semiconductor fabrication, is trade-secret process know-how. The recipe for a particular epitaxial growth run — the exact MOCVD conditions, the dopant profiles, the passivation chemistry — exists in an engineer's notebook and a fab's process control system, not in a patent filing. Disclosure cuts both ways in a narrow market: it hands competitors a recipe they'd otherwise have to discover themselves. The rational strategy for a specialty III-V foundry is to patent the most obvious design-arounds and protect the rest as trade secrets.

This is, arguably, what Sivers has done. The accumulated process knowledge of the UK-based Sivers Photonics fab — formerly CST Global, acquired in 2017 — represents more than a decade of continuous development that can't be easily reconstructed from public filings. The counterargument is equally valid: trade-secret moats erode when engineers move. A well-funded competitor — a major Asian photonics house — could, in principle, hire the relevant process staff and rebuild the capability within three to five years. Against the timeline of the co-packaged optics market buildout, that's not an eternity.

## R&D Intensity, Obscured by Accounting

Sivers doesn't publish a clean R&D expense line, which makes direct spend quantification difficult. But the operating loss profile reveals the investment intensity. Under PCAOB-restated figures, Sivers posted a SEK 177.8M EBIT loss on SEK 306.6M of revenue in FY2025 — a -39% operating margin on a revenue base that grew 25% year-on-year. That's what a company looks like when it is running a small-batch specialty fab while funding custom engineering work for multiple ELS-module development partners simultaneously.

The PCAOB restatement added a material nuance. Among its drivers was the "impairment of previously capitalized development expenditures" — R&D costs Sivers had booked as future-period assets under Swedish K3 standards, written off as current-period expenses under US GAAP. The practical effect: FY2025 EBIT loss widened by SEK 36M versus the originally reported figure, and some of what appeared as a balance-sheet asset under Stockholm rules becomes a sunk cost in the US regulator's view. It also means reported earnings will be depressed through the entire investment phase, because R&D that Swedish accounting would spread forward gets expensed immediately.

## The Margin Horizon

Whether the IP and process investment ultimately generates returns depends on a scenario that hasn't arrived: production volume sufficient to spread fab fixed costs across enough units to drive operating leverage.

The most useful peer comparison is [MACOM Technology Solutions](https://www.macom.com/), which has historically achieved operating margins above 20% in its photonics business. MACOM's margin profile is the destination; Sivers' -39% is the departure point. The distance between them is measured in customer production ramps and the conversion of a $453M pipeline — up 64% year-on-year — into recognized revenue.

The POET Technologies collaboration, announced in September 2025, is the clearest near-term test case. Sivers DFB lasers combined with POET's optical interposer, targeting the external light source (ELS) market for co-packaged optics. CEO Vickram Vathulya framed it at the announcement:

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform."

The technical logic is real — POET's interposer handles the electronic-photonic integration; Sivers provides the laser source that neither POET nor its hyperscaler customers can readily source elsewhere at the required specification. Early prototypes were targeted for H1 2026; production readiness for end-2026. Neither milestone has been independently verified at this writing.

The $6.6M Year 2 NEMC grant awarded in May 2026 provides a different kind of signal. Non-dilutive US Department of Defense funding for defense infrastructure modernization isn't renewed for companies that missed Year 1 deliverables. The continuation implies technical milestones were met on the military-application side — limited evidence of execution credibility, but evidence nonetheless.

The IP moat, in the end, is best understood not as a patent count but as a combination: three fabrication disciplines integrated in a single facility, a decade-plus of process knowledge that isn't written down anywhere public, and collaborative relationships — imec, POET, Ayar Labs — that impose switching costs on the demand side. Whether that constitutes a durable chokepoint or a temporary technical lead is precisely what the next two years of customer ramps will determine.
